text:
Hey! I just want to echo what the other commenter said. 

Just to preface, she sounds like a completely normal child and you sound like a good parent. 

When I was a kid I was also a little chubbier and liked junk food, and between the bullying I got at school and having a mom with an active ED, I ended up developing anorexia when I was only about 7 or 8 years old, and I struggled with it into adulthood. And honestly my mom didn't make too many harmful comments towards me about my weight, but I saw how she talked about her own body and how she restricted and overexercised, and I started doing the same. I would just encourage you to model good habits/behaviors around food and exercise around her—not talking negatively about any part of your body or her body, not calling some foods "bad" and other foods "good", not talking about weight or carbs or fats or calories, etc. Just like every other kid, it's good for her to learn the difference between healthy and unhealthy food, but in the context of what will help her grow, what makes her stronger, what feeds her brain, etc.—foods that are good for her body, but not just because they'll make her lose weight. Maybe you can start a habit of cooking together or regularly trying out new foods?

But again, she sounds totally normal, and I think every kid is like that. Eventually they get older, they grow a bit (and probably thin out a little in the process), and they learn moderation. But in the end, it matters more that she has a healthy relationship to food and to her body than that she's thin. 

I don't think there's anything wrong with you for thinking like this, though, and you shouldn't be too hard on yourself for it. You clearly love your daughter and you're staying aware of how your relationship with ED affects her, and that's all a kid could ask for.

So I know EXACTLY what you mean by this being purely OCD driven. I too used to compulsively do hour long circuits, 30k steps a day etc. and go to bed crying and wake up crying every day knowing I "had to" do it all again. I don't know if you can relate to this part but a lot of it was because I had very bad anxiety and no other coping mechanisms. text:
It’s going to be hard, but it’s worth it. I did not last long in residency, I moved to a partial program where I went home at night, but from my 3 days in residency… my program had stages, and your first stage doesn’t last long but it’s the most restrictive. You won’t get a lot of privacy until the staff knows you better, stuff like bathrooms will be locked and monitored- they will measure your waste after you use the toilet. You will likely get some choice in what you eat, but not much leeway with how much. Most likely they will scale up your portions over a couple weeks though, depending on your situation at least if you are like me and just not able to tolerate full servings immediately.  If you can’t finish meals they will replace what’s needed with supplements, but this can prolong your time in lower stages of the program.  In my program they got us up at 5:30 for vitals, weights, and medication and then we could choose to try to go back to sleep, relax or shower until 7 am breakfast. Staff was very kind and try their best to make it as positive as it can be but you will witness people having very hard days, and yet I found my fellow patients to be incredibly empathetic and kind and helped me get familiar with the center. As you moved up in levels you gained privileges like visitors (that’s only restricted for the first couple days at mine, because you were restricted to the group room off hours until they know you are medically stabilized enough and won’t bolt or hurt yourself if unsupervised), closing the door to your room and the bathroom, passes to leave the center for approved outings, nature walks etc. no bags or closed containers allowed and no wearing hoodies with pockets while eating so pack a pull over or something without pockets for those times. No mirrors or glass including the ones in makeup pallets in your room. No sharp objects or scarves in your room. Honestly I didn’t even care about my makeup there, nobody else did either and i probably wouldn’t bring most of it if I were to go again. Headphones are a lifesaver, and if you are an adult you will be able to keep your phone, but minors should bring an mp3 player or whatever that isn’t WiFi connected if you want music. They will say they have art supplies but it’s  limited, if you enjoy that I’d bring some of your own as well as books and other entertainment. I found it hard to sleep because I was cold and wished I’d packed a heavier blanket. They will do night checks- the good nurses are subtle but some don’t seem to care if they wake you up so I’d suggest ear plugs and maybe a sleeping mask to limit that disruption. 

The best advice I think I have is to know it won’t be easy and it won’t be fun the first couple days, but it IS worth it if it’s what you need. And you will get in what you put in- and if you dedicate yourself to healing and trust the process you will get through it as fast as you possibly can. Try to resist the urge to fight the program even if you’re frustrated, because it’s only hurting you and slowing you down if you do. 

You will also meet some wonderful people and you will probably find yourself caring about them very much. Embrace that community and solidarity, but be wary of picking up friends in that place you take with you after if they are not also dedicated to their healing. It can sound harsh, but you can subliminally trigger and sabotage each other too because you understand each others demons. You’ll learn a lot about both trust and vulnerability here, as well as lessons in letting go. 

This I hope will be a good thing you are grateful you did. Be proud of yourself, getting here takes an incredible amount of strength ♥️

General criteria for calling an ambulance or presenting to emergency immediately: 
- chest pain 
- shortness of breath 
- heart palpitations, low hr <50, or tachycardia (high heart rate >120)
- dizziness in general but also on standing
- food refusal for 3 or more days
- BMI <13 
- suicidal ideation/thoughts of self harm
- distress that cannot be managed with usual coping strategies 

Different states have different guidelines, I’m happy to direct you to one that is relevant to your state

First of all, well done Dad for being proactive in a loving and supportive way. 

I struggled with an ED from the time I was 15 and at 46 I finally went into intensive outpatient care. Here’s what I learned:
1. EDs are about coping skills, not food (just like other addictions).
2. Focusing on good vs bad foods perpetuates the problem. I would recommend the book Intuitive Eating by Trimble and Resch (4th Edition). Wrap your mind around those concepts…maybe read it together.
3. Beware of a hyper focus on exercise. Some of us were put on exercise restriction b/c it also became disordered.
4. Look up the National Eating Disorder Association (NEDA)…it’s full of lots of gems.
5. Whatever ANY of you do, do NOT comment on looks (body, dress, muscle growth, hair, etc.) at all….to her or others. Comments seemingly positive or negative have the same result…they focus on IMAGE. Body image is deathly. As a society we need to value other attributes. I have even gone as far with people as saying, “FYI, b/c “image” is a harmful hyperfixation we have as a society, I will not be commenting on this. I care more about what YOU think of yourself and that is all that should matter.” It’s really foreign to humans. 

Finally, I went to the Emily Program in Seattle. I can’t tell you how profound an experience that was for me. Other girls had been to some others and found them to cause more harm. Look up their philosophy, methodologies, and compare it to what’s available to your daughter.

I wish you all the best of luck. It’s a LONG road and triggers happen. Knowing you are supported by those who make a true effort to learn along side of you is paramount to thriving. text:
Hello, (24 f been in recovery since 2014)

I've been through so many stages on this journey and I've definitely been there. I think an inportant question that may help is to ask yourself, am I really full, or am I just "emotionally" full? 

Due to the mind-gut connection (thank you vagus nerve!) It is absolutely impossible to separate our thoughts, and feelings from our eating experience. That's why emotional eating isn't inherently bad, because food  can serve a very real comforting purpose in times of stress. This is adaptive in nature. However, when you are someone who has an eating disorder, your mind is likely still very sick if you are still associating feelings of guilt with the eating experience. Conditioned and unesesary feelings of guilt surrounding eating can CREATE stress which can take away appetite temporarily. 

Being emotionally full and having an ED may look like:
Thought: "I already ate x,y, z today"
Feeling: guilt 
Physical sensation: body feels tense, full 
Behavior/consequence of initial thought:
Stops eating too soon, gets really hungry later 

What I just did right here is an example of CBT (Cognitive behavioral therapy) since our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are all interconnected it can be helpful in exploring how certain thoughts fuel undeserved feelings and behaviors and working towards changing those thoughts through reframing them.

Example of a thought reframe:

ED thought: "I feel so FAT and UGLYYYY"

Re-frame: "Fat is not a feeling and fat is not a dirty word." 

The only way I was able to conquer feelings of guilt when eating is literally through redramimg my thoughts, this re-wiring my brain. 

Seeing intuitive eating dieticians have helped to debunk and reframe diet culture myths as well.
Helpful guilt reframes I've learned:

1. "Despite what diet-culture tries to advertise to you, guilt is NOT an ingredient."

2. "less calories= less energy and who wants less energy?"

3. "Food does NOT hold morality. There are NO good vs. Bad foods. ALL food holds nutritional value. The body processes all foods the same. ALL food fits."

4. "Every body is a GOOD body."

5. "My weight and appearance are the absolute LEAST interesting thing about me."

Big hugs— I’ve been there. Okay, to start— you didn’t do this to yourself. You have an eating disorder and it is hurting you enough without you blaming yourself. The number one message I want you to hear is that this isn’t your fault, and you deserve to be gentle with yourself and get help. Second, you should look into seeing a nutritionist to help you with all the stuff you have wrapped around food. They’ll be able to help you figure out how to get the nutrients you need. You should also get a therapist— the therapist is the one who will be able to help with the mental health part of the disorder, the “can’t seem to eat” part. My nutritionist said she sees so many people who see her and think she can heal the ED, but you really need therapy to work on the reasons behind your ED behaviors, because ultimately eating disorders are a type of coping mechanism for something deeper.
Also, along the lines of being gentle with yourself, let’s try to stop calling food good or bad. Right now, you’re having trouble eating; all food is good food. You have a history of restriction, so it’s completely normal to be starving, grab the fastest thing, and then feel terrible about it. It’s also completely normal that you’re fatigued- you’re starving! Also completely normal that your digestion is out of whack and you’re bloating- this is what happens after restriction. I spent SIX YEARS cutting out any food that I thought would make me bloat, and finally I saw a nutritionist and learned that everything I thought was a food intolerance was actually just digestion. 

These are still early days for you— this shit is hard and takes a long time to work on. Knowing that you’re struggling is a HUGE step and you’re doing great already. This won’t happen overnight, and there are always periods where the ED voice is louder than your recovery voice, but you can do this. You haven’t permanently ruined your body, it’s just trying to adapt to what you’ve been struggling with. Our bodies are amazing and capable of dealing with ups and downs, and over time it will change as you start to get better.

1. Probiotics! I take the webber's naturals probiotic once daily. Contact a doctor first but for women they are generally recommended. I have noticed a huge decrease in bloating in as little as a month of taking these.

2. Walking - if you feel comfortable doing so. There are walking pads and treadmills on my uni campus I use all the time. These also have helped me with dizziness caused by a drop in BP (any exercise will temporarily raise blood pressure and alleviate these symptoms). In terms of bloating and gas, just 45 mins of walking helps GREATLY.

3. Smaller meals, more often. Depending on your meal plan, this could help with the bloating. However take this with a grain of salt because this is a personalized meal plan from my dietitian.

text:
I recently started recovery on my own. Last year I had therapy and it didn’t work out. I’m back on the waiting list but I realized I am the only one who can make me better. I have an advantage of course because I already had some tools from therapy last year (and another time many years ago). 

I have AN b/p. I never went a day without binging and often even multiple times a day. I thought I could never do it. 

What helped me most was being brutally honest with myself. I had to stop acting like I would magically wake up one day and do better. I needed structure, repetition, and a lot of trial and error.

What I did was eat more consistently during the day, even when my hunger cues were a mess. Make a list of “safe enough” foods and meals that I could fall back on. Plan my evenings better, because that was my most dangerous time. Learn the difference between real hunger, feeling full/bloated, and emotional panic. Stop making every slip mean “well, the day is ruined anyway”, focus on reducing b/p frequency first, not on being perfect immediately

I also used ChatGPT a lot in my recovery. Not as a replacement for therapy, but as support in between. It helped me reflect, calm down, make meal plans, reality-check ED thoughts, and stay on track when I was panicking or wanted to binge/purge. Sometimes I just needed something or someone to help me pause and not escalate. On a side note; You have to be totally honest with the tool and I have the paid version, I am not sure how it works with the free version. It’s still around 20 euros a month but much cheaper than a real therapist and it’s always there when you need it. It’s literally the voice of reason for me. 

I still think professional help is important if you can get it, but if you cannot afford therapy right now, you shouldn’t think that you are helpless. There are still things you can do. But it will be very hard, absolutely!

The biggest change for me was accepting that recovery is not only “mental work” first and then food later or the other way around. For me both had to happen together. My brain got better when I kept showing my body more safety and consistency, even when I did not feel ready.

In therapy they often told me to distract myself as much as possible when I had binge urges. But I personally found that distraction alone was not enough. What helped me more was slowing down and really paying attention to what my body was signaling. Sometimes I was not actually dealing with a “random urge,” but with hunger, fullness panic, exhaustion, restriction earlier in the day, or feeling emotionally overwhelmed. Learning to notice that made a big difference.

This is a long message, but I hope it can be a little bit useful for you (or anyone else here)

I went through 2 pregnancies with an ED. Your body will do everything to support the growing baby, including siphoning nutrients from your own bones (incl teeth). I learned this the hard way with the first pregnancy and was able to make better choices with the second. I wish I’d sought out therapy. 

I would tell her to ask the docs for a minimum calorie goal for each trimester, and work to meet that because chronic deficiency can cause developmental problems with the baby’s organs.

eta: Also, purging behaviors can cause dangerous electrolyte imbalances for mom and fetus. Blood volume increases, and the heart has to work overtime. So, make sure she at least has a back-up plan to restore electrolytes in whatever solution she feels safe drinking (do a little research on what ratios of sodium and potassium are safe during pregnancy).

text:
Hello, guys, I am one of the mods that approves requests and handles the subreddit. I will be speaking from my own point of view and not of all mods when I refer to myself.

A post like this has been long overdue. The thing is that while this post is extremely well written and informative it could also push the idea that those who post "Do I have an ED" most likely don't have an eating disorder but a disordered eating pattern. The problem is that we don't know and that none of us can confirm if you have an eating disorder. This post is certainly one that comes from a very good place and has no intentions of nullifying anyone's ED or disordered eating pattern. But if we were to deflect all requests from people who haven't been diagnosed then this sub would have way less participants. Less participants means less answers, less support, etc ...

Requests like "Do I have an ED" happen a lot. I'd say about 60% of all requests are questions if they could have their post because they are concerned they might be developing an eating disorder or that they suspect they have an eating disorder and are seeking validation of some kind.  A common thought with anyone who struggles with any disorder is:  *Am I hurting bad enough to seek help? Am I "sick enough"*. This is one of the reasons as to why we allow these posts to come through. We never know which post might "save a life".

The majority of the time I reply with the same kind of response - I even have a prefab reply that I copy and paste for those posts - and while that blocks a whole bunch of the requests I can't help but think... There has to be a reason as to why we are getting so many requests about this. What I have been told regularly is that some people do not have the ability to seek help. Regardless of money, some requests talk about the OP not being able to speak to their doctor or legal guardians about this. Others seek help for beloved ones. 


We, the mods, know that allowing these posts wont fix anyone's (possible) ED. None of us, mods or readers, can actually help diagnose an eating disorder. Even if some of us were licensed professionals. 

That being said, I think this post definitely brings up a great point. The original intent of this sub was for people to have questions about eating disorders like:

* How to deal with the common struggles about eating disorders

* How to deal with certain situations. (Public eating, how to tell someone you trust about your struggles)

* How to seek help

* etc...

The sub has changed from mostly asking questions about eating disorders to people mainly venting and people who seek validation. This is due to lack of moderation on certain aspects and the fact that we've grown a whole lot. The lack of moderation is something we have to speak about internally. 

How we will move forward, I don't know. I am however open for ANYONE to openly DM me how to improve things or share their experiences. I really want this sub to be a safe, informative place with a clear purpose. Cause now it is somewhat all over the place.

I am also available on our Discord server. You can find the link in each auto moderator reply, by checking the sidebar or clicking on this link: https://discord.gg/ShRD55t

I wish you all the best.

You will make friends! Not everyone gets along all of the time, it is close quarters and stressful situations but at the end of the day you’re all there with the same goal, to get better. 

My program was scheduled with downtime in between each meal and snack and about 3 groups a day. Mixed into the down time was individual sessions but those were only once a week. 

We did have a set time to go up to the bedrooms but had about 2 hours to shower and unwind before lights out at around 10-11. 

Meals depending on your program. Mine followed intuitive eating ideals that we gradually worked up to. So we started off with a circle menu for the first week or so and then got to start creating our own meals a little bit. We’d meal plan every 3 days. My nutritionist would throw in some challenges like I had a whole day where I got to on the spot decide what I wanted. Dinners were pretty much always just two options, meat or vegan of a similar thing. 

There will pretty much always be at least one person who works there around. They might not always be able to answer your questions or things specific to your treatment but can get the answers for you or set up a time to talk with your team. And they are there to help you work through whatever you’re feeling anxious about. 

Definitely keep the mindset of this being an adventure. You’re there to take care of yourself, learn about yourself, and grow I hope you get everything you need out of this!

It’s also worth noting that their body is a significant part of their livelihood, so it’s essentially like a normal person having a job - for them fitness is a significant part of their job. All this is in addition to them having access to drugs/pharmaceuticals/supplements for anything from appetite suppression to mood elevation to stimulants, etc. Another relevant point is that there is a difference between maintaining a low weight and trying to lose weight when you are already thin. Someone who is already (for example) 100lbs can maintain that weight even eating 1500kcal+ per day, especially if they are exercising - this is vastly different than someone with a severe ED, who is perpetually trying to lose weight and thus constantly in a deficit. 

Likewise while many celebrities are thin, it is relatively rare to see them maintaining sub 17.5 BMIs for extended periods - and those that do seem to make relatively few public appearances - obviously there are a few outliers and I’m sure genetics can also play a role - even celebrities in general make up a very small portion of the population. I went through a similar phase after anorexia recovery (around 14 years old and am now 24). After recovery, I was eating pretty healthy and what I thought was how other people normally ate and regained weight to a “normal weight.” However I was still super hungry and started doing the same thing as you’re describing. I’d recommend looking up and reading about mental hunger in recovery (NOT “emotionally eating” or any of those diet culture terms). Your body may still be craving certain “off limit” foods for nutrients they provide (I craved cheese a lot - fats, calcium, vitamin D). Even if you’re getting all your nutrients in now, it may be reasonable for your body to want even more in order to help rebuild any leftover damage the ED may have caused, and to make your body feel safe again in case another period of restriction (or famine) comes along. Definitely not a choice you’re deciding to make, more like years and years of evolution.

The only thing that helped me was listening to that mental hunger, and eating the “off limits” foods and then making them part of my daily life. For me, if I was craving cheese, I wouldn’t try to make myself eat a “normal balanced meal” - I’d just listen to my body and eat cheese for the meal lol (and maybe some other things) and eventually it got better. But yeah it was a couple of painful, frustrating and shameful months. I felt guilty a lot and wanted to go back to restricting, but the cycle will continue for years unless you let your body do what it needs to, even if it doesn’t make sense to you, doctors or researchers.

I think it's an individual thing.  People can be \*really\*  deep into their EDs and their blood tests come back looking fine.  As far as vitamins go, I suspect that normal vitamin pills might keep most people on the level with those ?

But the thing you'll want to watch out for with bulimia is potassium  (K+) shortages.  Purging can really knock a person's K+ levels out of whack.   Potassium is also the one that gives people heart  attacks,  or other sorts of heart rhythm problems, and can be the main cause of mortality with bulimia. 

K+ problems can show up in blood tests, and if knowledgeable professionals  are going to get you checked out, and know that you purge, that's definitely going to be something they would check for.

If a person's levels are low, they can give people an infusion via an IV drip, that helps get their levels back on course.

I agree with what others said in lurking in spaces. I also suggest considering there's more EDs than just anorexia and bulimia, there's also binge eating disorder (often misunderstood or misrepresented) and orthorexia just to name a couple. There's also EDNS (eating disorder, not specified) and different subtypes of anorexia. 

I also think that watching some existing media and dissecting the good from the bad representation would be beneficial. For example there's To The Bone which I feel has a pretty realistic view of ED sufferers but isn't without its own cringe. There's also Starving in Suburbia which is one that many people make fun of for good reason lol but it has some good parts in it too. There's lots of "classics" but these two are the most "modern" ones I know of. 

 Some things to consider that I feel like other media portrayals don't seem to understand:

\-Men can have EDs too

\-EDs don't just affect white teenaged girls

\-Adults can have EDs and EDs can start in adulthood

\-EDs can go hidden until it becomes obvious physically because by nature they're secretive

\-Relapses are common (Might be interesting to write from a perspective of someone going through a relapse rather than one entering the ED)

\-EDs can be competitive sometimes literally

\-EDs can be started from trauma not just the desire to lose weight or be skinny 

\-EDs can stem from other mental illnesses (like OCD and ADHD) 

Suggested reading:  
Wintergirls

Fat Chance if your characters are younger

Thin (autobiography)

I'm Glad My Mom Died   


If you have questions regarding BED specifically I don't mind answering.   


 Also OP please take care to remember to separate what you're seeing from yourself. Don't let yourself believe in any of it and remember anything you might see glorified or trivialized by people with EDs are the words of people suffering from mental illness.  Don't let yourself normalize anything you read or see and if you find it's affecting your own point of view take a step back. Not that you can "give" yourself an ED but you can normalize disordered behaviors and internalize certain things and affect your health and wellbeing if you're not vigilant.

I have severe POTS & ARFID & chronic pain 

Here’s a few things I recommend;

1. Ignore your doctor. Most people with POTS find that restrictive eating including minor deficits worsens their POTS a lot. If your POTS is currently unmanaged/bad, you do not want to add more stress to your body

2. Ignore your doctor pt. 2; please don’t cut out all carbs. While carbs can be a trigger to some (not all) POTS patients, if it isn’t correlated to your triggers for POTS then ignore it. Even if it is a trigger, fed is best. Otherwise, I recommend eating carb-heavy meals before bed/later in day rather than early morning, which is the inverse of what a lot of people tend to recommend for healthy individuals! But I find carbs in the morning triggers my POTS more throughout the day. Obviously, it’s trial and error, find what works best for you

3. Follow the CHOP protocol. It can help with making sure you don’t physically regress and is what helps a lot of people who are debilitated / disabled by POTS to become more functional. Since it’s disability friendly and aims for low or *no* impact, it should work for you

4. Similarly, look into no-impact exercises or extremely low-impact exercises. They may be targeted to the elderly but it will help. Even if you only do 1 minute a day, that’s better than none. Ideally you’d be doing 5-10 mins daily. If you can, get a POTS informed physical therapist. Your chronic pain from that incident sounds abnormal, but a lot of normal physical therapists aren’t POTS informed and may not help properly

5. Have you been checked for gastroparesis? GP & POTS go hand in hand and what you say about hunger cues reminds me of that. If you haven’t already been checked, it may be worthwhile to look into 

6. Medical grade compression long socks / leggings. Seriously it’s a game changer. 

While it’s unfortunate things have been so rough, it’s amazing that you’re still getting by. Really, it’s not easy managing chronic health issues, and you are doing your absolute best

Best of luck

text:
ED can impact sleep in negative way. During sleep, our body releases hormones, which control hunger and fullness and when you have bad quality sleep for a long time, it affects all of your hormones. Also with long term sleep deprivation, body releases cortisol (stress hormone) during the day more,  that's why you probably feel bad after eating.

I don't have great advice, since ny ED affects my sleep too (I am very tired in the evening,  but I wake up at 4-5 am everyday even when I don't have enough deep sleep). But here are some tips, which helped me to make it at least bearable:
1. Sleep schedule- try to stick to strict sleep schedule and try to go to bed at the same time everyday. Even when you couldn't fall asleep, try to stay in bed, breathe slowly, try to make it as relaxing as possible (soothing music, ventilated room etc)
2. Melatonin- low dose of melatonin could help improve quality of sleep, so even if you are unable to sleep for 8 hours, sleep itself should be better and body will be little bit more relaxed.
3. Food- this is tricky, because changing/restricting food when you have ED is not always possible, but it definitely helps if you don't go to bed hungry, but also very full. If possible, try to eat 2 hours before going to bed and your last meal should be little bit lighter (for example fat takes long time to digest, so you might feel restless after eating fries before bed). It also helps to eat throughout the day, so you won't feel super hungry in the evening. But I know that this is the hardest part when you have ED.
4. Creatine- some studies found, that supplementing creatine helps body function better after bad sleep
5. Excercise- relaxing excercise like yoga before bed time might help body to feel relaxed and tired.

Again, these are things, that help ME, it might not work for you. Stay safe and I hope your sleep would get better.

I didn’t actually get treatment until I was 15 years old at an eating disorder treatment facility. Eating disorders require a specific treatment as it is a speciality in the field. The current evidence based treatment for ALL eating disorder diagnosis is a team of psychiatrist (for medication management), intuitive eating dietician (helps debunk diet-culture myths and food labeling and food rules and helps to view nutrition from a more nuetral and INTUITIVE lens and we were all born intuitive eaters with the ability to both TRUST and connect and listen to body. Disordered eating breeds the opposite: body distrust, fear, and disconnection. They help explore relationship with food and barriers to eating which usually is rooted in fear and cognitive distortions) and then of course a therapist that specializes in eating disorders as it is a specialty. 

It sounds like your son already has an extensive history with mental health and mental health is complex and often these things DO overlap. I just want to say that from an outsider view—you have done so much already and are a great father and support. It really shows you care for your son. 

Obviously you have to get evaluated and diagnosed by a professional to confirm but it sounds like your son could be struggling with ORTHOREXIA: Orthorexia is an unhealthy focus on eating in a healthy way. Eating nutritious food is good, but if you have orthorexia, you obsess about it to a degree that can damage your overall well-being.

Orthorexia Symptoms

If you have orthorexia, you might:

Worry about food quality. High levels of concern about the quality and source of foods you eat could lead to anxiety.
Avoid going out to eat or avoid eating food prepared by others out of fear that foods you don’t prepare yourself won’t meet your standards.
Fear sickness. You worry about how “clean” food is or if it’s “bad” for your health.
Show physical signs of malnutrition. When you limit the variety of foods you eat, you may not get all the nourishment you need. You could lose weight as a result.
Bury yourself in food research. It’s one thing to spend a few minutes scanning a product label or surfing the web for more information on ingredients. But with orthorexia, you may spend hours thinking about food and planning meals.
Refuse to eat a broad range of foods. It’s normal to avoid some foods because you don’t like the way they taste or the way they make you feel. But with orthorexia, you might decide to drop whole categories of foods from your diet. For example, you might stop eating grains; or any foods with preservatives, gluten, or sugar; or all foods that just don’t seem “healthy."
Fear losing control. You feel that you’re doing the right thing by eating healthy. But you may also be afraid that eating even one meal you didn’t prepare -- including dinner at a restaurant -- can be disastrous.
Be overly critical of your friends’ food choices. At the same time, you may have no rational explanation for your own.
Find yourself in a vicious circle. Your preoccupation with food causes you to bounce between self-love and guilt as you change and restrict your diet.

I'll be the dissenting voice here.

First though, I have to note that I never ventured into life-threatening territory with my weight or attitudes about it, but I do have an anorexia diagnosis. I also never had residential or inpatient care – it was all outpatient through an eating disorder therapist.

I found that early in my recovery when I stopped counting calories, I justified eating far less than I needed. I had an attidute of 'I'm eating intuitively, and stopping when I'm full' which basically meant very little food at all. I had no accountability or any real or positive gauge for how much I was eating, so I just ate less. Even in recovery, I was still a cyclist and still burning through calories, and I wasn't replacing them properly, so I continued to lose power and overall energy.

I decided to start counting calories to keep myself from losing weight, but also to keep myself accountable and even gain weight. I successfully did all of those things while also counting calories early on in my recovery. It was hard to break away from fixating on the numbers so much and having new or 'fear' foods, but over time it became far easier. Also, I didn't want to spend the out-of-pocket money on a dietician to set up a meal plan or anything due to the cost – it's not covered by my insurance.

This is definitely not for everyone though, so don't take this as an automatic justification to count calories in your case. It worked for me for a number of reasons that are unique to my own life, so it may not apply to others. Sometimes people in all sorts of supportive communities paint some things as black and white, which is never quite true. While yes, counting calories is generally not advised, there are cases where it can work.

tone: empathetic, direct, kind

You are taking what she has told you as a person attack on your intelligence, capability/capacity, and/or your identity. You've used the disordered eating to shore up and protect hurt, harmed parts of you. And maybe also parts of you that you don't like, or feel helpless to change. Taking down those protections you made is required part of getting better.

> I do not [feel better when I do the opposite of my ED behaviors]. I feel like shit.

Is it all mental symptoms of feeling like shit, or do you have physical symptoms, or both? What symptoms do you have?

> I still am obsessive [even after gaining weight]. Now I just feel obsessive *and* defeated.

You didn't stumble into ED at this level of neurosis immediately. It took time to get here. It takes time to get out.

> "That's your eating disordered voice. That's not who you are"  
- um, you've met me 2 months ago and we've talked 4 times. You don't know who I am really.

There's nothing new under the sun. Did you know that 80% of autistic people also have some kind of gastrointestinal problem? Or that ~90% of r\*pe victims are female, and ~99% of perpetrators are male? Or that hearing loss is linked to diabetes and isolation? Things get linked to other things through causality, not whimsy.  
[People with eating disorders sound very similar and do similar things.](https://www.centralcoasttreatmentcenter.com/blog-1/6-common-cognitive-distortions-behind-eating-disorders) You're having a very yes-no (black&white) thought that because you've only met her four times she doesn't know you. She doesn't need to know *you* in order to know what *ED* sounds like and does, because you are not alone in your experience. Thousands and thousands of people before you have had the same struggles you're facing. Not all of them were successfully treated, but the similarities have been reported enough to know whether it is "you" or "the disease" talking. It's not an attack on what you're thinking, what you're feeling, or how hard this is for you. There is no such thing as just being stronger and getting over this. The walls you shored up have to come down and you can't fight and be defensive. Only after that can you start to have healthy walls that aren't made up on neurotic, compulsive, etc. building blocks.

This might not be the right person to help you, but you cannot get better without actually changing and going through the very hard and very painful process of accepting that the disordered eating is harming you, and you working to get rid of it. You aren't perfect and if anyone expects you to be, they're wrong. If you don't face your (however subconscious) thought that the ED is better than dealing with what's really hurting you, then you'll face the same problem with a new therapist. What your therapist is saying does not seem incorrect, but maybe they are not empathetic enough for you to be able to accept their help.

edit: OP deleted their post. They're not ready to take down the walls. Such a shame. 😔 I'm glad I've helped some others in their place though.

You should see a doctor as well, to get your labwork done, because when you stop eating, you can deplete nutrients. Go for super easy comfort foods, and things you can nibble on whenever the headaches and things start, just some nibbles every hour until you can work up to a full snack, and slowly begin eating meals again. On their birthday, watch a show they used to like or movie, listen to a song they liked, and get a food they enjoyed and eat it, even if it's just a candy, something! i know it sounds so weird, but on that day i always like to just make sure i do something that would honor them or something they would like, it helps me (maybe not the case for you ) it helps me feel closer to them again. Another thing that helped, is you can post something online asking for anyone to send favorite memories of your brother to an email account you set up or wherever you use social media. I love hearing stories still, and having them compiled somewhere in a file or notebook are comforting whenever you need to have that time with them. 

I know it's hard, but again and again i want to make it clear that you are so strong for posting on here. Take your time eating, and talk to a doctor about the pain, sometimes you can give yourself stress ulcers and it's better to talk to a doctor about that. And most of all, be kind to yourself right now, grief suuuuuuuucks and it is painful.

So this isn't helpful to literally anyone, even people without an ED. 
For those without an ED who are struggling to lose weight, believe me, they have tried that (coming from someone who tried 900 different ways to lose fat healthily before my eating disorder relapse). People struggling with their weight, most of the time know this advice, have followed it.

People with an eating disorder, also know this advice. If it was only about losing fat, we probably wouldn't have an eating disorder. Eating disorders are far more complex than simply just eating healthy and everything is fixed. We have complex rules in our brain a lot of times that have zero real logic. We enjoy the high we get when we don't eat or see signs we are sick. We fixate on numbers and food. Sometimes we are illogical convinced that eating more than we are will cause us to gain weight (which in some cases I mean it does because the person is malnourished but not every case)

So really overall, and I apologize if this is rude, keep that advice to yourself. If someone opens up a conversation about healthy well balanced meal options, sure. But giving broad advice like eat three meals a day and do more cardio is the most redundant annoying advice for a not eating disorder person, and annoying as hell for an eating disorder person.
